title: Displacement Reactions

# Displacement Reactions

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Define displacement reactions
- Predict whether a displacement reaction will occur
- Write balanced equations for displacement reactions
- Explain displacement in terms of reactivity and electron transfer

## Introduction

A **displacement reaction** occurs when a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. These reactions help us confirm the reactivity series and have important industrial applications.

## Key Concepts

### What is Displacement?

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive metal "pushes out" a less reactive metal from its compound.

**General pattern:**
$$\text{Reactive metal} + \text{Less reactive metal compound} \rightarrow \text{Reactive metal compound} + \text{Less reactive metal}$$

### The Rule

**A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compound.**

If the metal is ABOVE the other in the reactivity series → reaction occurs
If the metal is BELOW the other in the reactivity series → no reaction

### Displacement in Solutions

**Example 1: Zinc in copper sulfate solution**
$$\text{Zn(s)} + \text{CuSO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$$

*Observations:*
- Blue solution fades/becomes colourless
- Brown/orange solid forms (copper)
- Zinc disappears/gets smaller
- Solution warms up (exothermic)

**Why it works:**
- Zinc is more reactive than copper
- Zinc atoms lose electrons more easily
- Zinc displaces copper from the solution

**Ionic equation:**
$$\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$$

[DIAGRAM: Before and after showing zinc strip in blue CuSO₄ solution, then colourless ZnSO₄ solution with copper coating]

**Example 2: Iron in copper sulfate solution**
$$\text{Fe(s)} + \text{CuSO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$$

*Observations:*
- Blue solution turns pale green
- Brown/orange solid forms on iron
- Iron appears to "rust" with copper

**Example 3: Magnesium in zinc chloride solution**
$$\text{Mg(s)} + \text{ZnCl}_2\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{Zn(s)}$$

### When No Reaction Occurs

**Example: Copper in zinc sulfate solution**

Copper + Zinc sulfate → **No reaction**

*Observations:*
- No colour change
- No solid forms
- Solution remains unchanged

**Why:** Copper is less reactive than zinc, so cannot displace it.

### Summary of Displacement Reactions

| Metal added | CuSO₄ (blue) | ZnSO₄ (colourless) | FeSO₄ (pale green) |
|-------------|--------------|--------------------|--------------|
| Mg | ✓ Reaction | ✓ Reaction | ✓ Reaction |
| Zn | ✓ Reaction | ✗ No reaction | ✓ Reaction |
| Fe | ✓ Reaction | ✗ No reaction | ✗ No reaction |
| Cu | ✗ No reaction | ✗ No reaction | ✗ No reaction |

### Displacement and Electron Transfer

Displacement reactions are **redox reactions:**

**Example: Zinc + Copper sulfate**

**Oxidation half-equation:**
$$\text{Zn} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^-$$
(Zinc loses electrons - oxidation)

**Reduction half-equation:**
$$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$$
(Copper ions gain electrons - reduction)

- The more reactive metal (Zn) is **oxidised**
- The less reactive metal ions (Cu²⁺) are **reduced**

### Displacement with Halogens

Displacement also works with non-metals like halogens:

**Reactivity order:** Chlorine > Bromine > Iodine

$$\text{Cl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{2KBr(aq)} \rightarrow \text{2KCl(aq)} + \text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$$

*Observations:* Colourless/pale green solution turns orange/brown (bromine formed)

$$\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{2KI(aq)} \rightarrow \text{2KBr(aq)} + \text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$$

*Observations:* Orange solution turns brown/black (iodine formed)

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Predict whether a reaction occurs when iron is added to silver nitrate solution. If yes, write the equation.

**Solution:**
- Iron is above silver in the reactivity series
- Iron is more reactive than silver
- Reaction WILL occur
$$\text{Fe(s)} + \text{2AgNO}_3\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Fe(NO}_3\text{)}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{2Ag(s)}$$

---

**Example 2:** Will copper displace zinc from zinc chloride solution? Explain.

**Solution:**
- Copper is below zinc in the reactivity series
- Copper is less reactive than zinc
- A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one
- **No reaction** will occur

---

**Example 3:** Write the ionic equation and half-equations for magnesium displacing copper from copper sulfate.

**Solution:**

**Full equation:**
$$\text{Mg(s)} + \text{CuSO}_4\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{MgSO}_4\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$$

**Ionic equation:**
$$\text{Mg(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$$

**Half-equations:**
- Oxidation: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
- Reduction: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking any metal can displace any other
- **Correct:** Only a MORE reactive metal can displace a LESS reactive one

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to balance equations (especially with silver: 2AgNO₃)
- **Correct:** Check that charges and atoms are balanced

- **Mistake:** Not recognising displacement as a redox reaction
- **Correct:** The reactive metal is oxidised; the metal ion is reduced

## Practice Questions

1. Define the term 'displacement reaction'. (2 marks)

2. Predict whether a reaction will occur in each case:
   a) Zinc in magnesium sulfate solution
   b) Magnesium in iron(II) sulfate solution
   c) Copper in silver nitrate solution
   (3 marks)

3. Write a balanced equation for the reaction between magnesium and copper chloride solution. (2 marks)

4. A student adds iron filings to copper sulfate solution. Describe what the student would observe. (3 marks)

5. Write the ionic equation and half-equations for the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate. Label which half-equation shows oxidation and which shows reduction. (4 marks)

6. Explain, in terms of electron transfer, why zinc can displace copper from copper sulfate but copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate. (4 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Displacement reaction | A reaction where a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element |
| Ionic equation | An equation showing only the ions that change during a reaction |
| Half-equation | An equation showing either the oxidation or reduction part of a reaction |
| Spectator ions | Ions that don't change during a reaction (e.g., SO₄²⁻) |

## Summary

- **Displacement:** A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one
- More reactive metal + compound of less reactive metal → **reaction occurs**
- Less reactive metal + compound of more reactive metal → **no reaction**
- Displacement reactions are **redox reactions:**
  - More reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons)
  - Less reactive metal ion is reduced (gains electrons)
- Observations: colour changes, solid forms, metal disappears, temperature rises
- Works for halogens too: Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂
